title: Readonly anonymous classes
summary: PHP 8.3 extends the `readonly` class modifier to anonymous class declarations (`new readonly class {...}`), so a throwaway anonymous class can get the same every-property-readonly treatment PHP 8.2 gave named readonly classes.
new_code_policy: On a feature ceiling of 8.3 or above, when an anonymous class's declared properties are all (or will all be) readonly, write `new readonly class {...}` instead of marking each property individually with `readonly`. Never emit `readonly` on an anonymous class declaration while the feature ceiling is 8.2 or lower: PHP 8.2 already has readonly classes for named classes (see `language.readonly_classes`), but the modifier is a parse error on an anonymous class declaration specifically until 8.3, so it fails to parse the entire file, not just that one expression.
existing_code_policy: Do not bulk-convert every anonymous class whose properties happen to all be readonly; collapse it to `readonly class` only when it is already being touched for another reason, and only after confirming the feature ceiling is 8.3 or newer - unlike the named-class case, there is no 8.2 fallback rendering for an anonymous class, so introducing this modifier on a lower ceiling breaks the file outright rather than merely losing a nicety. Do not apply it to an anonymous class that declares (or inherits from a class it extends) any untyped or static property, or that needs `#[AllowDynamicProperties]`, since a readonly class forbids all three.
guideline: Once the feature ceiling reaches PHP 8.3, prefer `new readonly class {...}` over repeating `readonly` on every property of an anonymous class whose properties are uniformly readonly - the same simplification `language.readonly_classes` already recommends for named classes, now extended to anonymous ones. Never emit it below a feature ceiling of 8.3, where it is a parse error.
details: PHP 8.3 (UPGRADING-8.3.0, "2. New Features" -> Core: "Anonymous classes may now be marked as readonly.") extends the readonly-class modifier introduced for named classes in PHP 8.2 (see the shipped `language.readonly_classes` rule) to anonymous class declarations: `new readonly class {...}` is now valid, as is `new readonly class(...) extends Foo {...}` and every other anonymous-class form. This is purely an extension of where the modifier may be written, not a new or different feature: everything `language.readonly_classes` documents about what `readonly` means on a class - every property the class declares becomes readonly, and the class is rejected outright if it declares an untyped property ("Readonly property ... must have type", confirmed locally) or a static property ("Static property ... cannot be readonly", confirmed locally) - applies identically whether the class is named or anonymous, and is not restated here. What changes in 8.3 is purely syntactic: on PHP 8.2, `readonly` in front of the `class` keyword of an anonymous class declaration is not recognized in that position and is a parse error, failing the entire file it appears in rather than being merely an unsupported runtime construct - there is no 8.2 fallback rendering for `new readonly class`, unlike features that only lose a nicety on an older engine. This makes the construct feature-axis gated: it must never be emitted unless the feature ceiling (the lowest PHP minor the code must still run on) is already 8.3 or above. Anonymous classes marked readonly are most useful exactly where anonymous classes already are - small throwaway value objects and inline test doubles - which is why this is a distinct, worthwhile rule rather than an incidental corollary of `language.readonly_classes`.

after: return new readonly class ($fixedTime) implements ClockInterface {

notes: Everything about what readonly means on a class - every declared property becomes readonly, and the class may declare no untyped or static property - is documented by the shipped language.readonly_classes rule (PHP 8.2, named classes); this rule covers only the PHP 8.3 syntactic extension of where the modifier may be written, onto anonymous class declarations, and does not restate the underlying feature.

Confirmed locally on PHP 8.4.19: an anonymous readonly class that declares an untyped property is a compile-time fatal error ("Readonly property class@anonymous::$prop must have type"), and one that declares a static property is a compile-time fatal error ("Static property class@anonymous::$prop cannot be readonly") - the identical constraints language.readonly_classes documents for named readonly classes, unaffected by this rule's syntax extension.
Evidence: UPGRADING-8.3.0.txt, '2. New Features' -> Core: "Anonymous classes may now be marked as readonly."
